answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for an account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (sub-resources include Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases and .../mongodbCollections for Mongo API resources).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in Cosmos DB CLI group: az cosmosdb. Example to create a Mongo-compatible account: az cosmosdb create --name myDocDbAccount --resource-group myRG --locations regionName=westus2 --kind MongoDB. This is part of the core az CLI (az cosmosdb), not a separate extension.

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: resource of type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts' (set properties.apiProperties/kind or use capabilities to indicate MongoDB API); sample snippet: resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: accountName kind: 'MongoDB' properties: { ... } } . Terraform (AzureRM provider): use azurerm_cosmosdb_account to create the account, and use azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database / azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection to create DBs/collections. Example: resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "acct" location = "West US" offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.rg.name }

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: MongoDB-style URI. Example: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&authSource=admin&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. Notes: TLS/SSL must be enabled (ssl=true or tls=true), port typically 10255 for Cosmos Mongo API, username is often of the form '<user>@<account>' when using account keys, and retryWrites should be disabled for some Cosmos endpoints (retryWrites=false).

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Cosmos-style billing: throughput is billed in Request Units (RUs) per second when using provisioned throughput; there is also a serverless option in some regions where you pay per RU consumed. (For some managed MongoDB offerings on Azure there are also vCore-based SKUs, but the Mongo API on Cosmos historically uses RUs/throughput.)

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Common auth methods: MongoDB SCRAM (username/password) using the account primary keys, and Cosmos DB’s RBAC (Azure AD) for management plane. For MongoDB API clients you normally use SCRAM with the account key as password. Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) authentication for data-plane MongoDB connections is not the default — if supported it requires obtaining an AAD access token and using the MongoDB SASL/OAUTHBEARER mechanism or a provider-specific flow; typically you get a token with azure.identity and present it via the driver's SASL/OAUTHBEARER or a special connection option (implementation details vary and may be preview).

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for the application protocol (for Node.js use the official 'mongodb' driver or Mongoose ODM). There is not a special DocumentDB-specific driver for Mongo protocol data-plane access; the Azure-specific SDKs (azure-cosmos) are for the Cosmos SQL API/management, not for Mongo wire protocol access.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: (Based on the cluster description in the run environment) this DocumentDB endpoint exposes vector index types such as DiskANN, HNSW and IVF. The index is created with a Mongo-style createIndex call that specifies a vector index on the embedding field. Example (hypothetical syntax): db.plans.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', vector: { algorithm: 'HNSW', dims: 1536, metric: 'cosine' } }); Note: exact option names (algorithm, dims, metric) and placement are implementation-specific — treat this as the concrete command I would try first.

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text and hybrid (text + vector) search are done by integrating the DB with a search engine. For Azure this typically means using Azure Cognitive Search (push data via change feed or an indexer) or the service’s built-in vector index features if available. Hybrid ranking (text + vector) is performed in the search tier (Azure Cognitive Search or the DB’s vector search features) or in application code combining full-text results with vector similarity scores.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Compatibility follows the MongoDB API version that the account was configured for (historically Cosmos supported older versions like 3.6/4.0/4.2 and newer releases have added support up to more recent MongoDB server versions). Many managed MongoDB-API offerings do not support the entire MongoDB server feature set: some server-side JS, some storage-engine-specific features, and cross-partition multi-document transactions may be limited. Expect compatibility caveats; concrete server version and exact unsupported features depend on the account's configured MongoDB version. (If I must pick a default to act on: assume MongoDB 5.x API compatibility and avoid unsupported features such as server-side mapReduce and cross-partition multi-document transactions.)

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: Use the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator for local development. Docker image: mcr.microsoft.com/cosmosdb/linux/azure-cosmos-emulator:latest (or the Windows emulator on Windows). The Mongo-compatible endpoint on the emulator uses the same Mongo port as the cloud endpoint (typically 10255) and requires TLS; confirm the exact exposed port from the emulator docs but try 10255 first.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Yes — the MongoDB API supports change streams/CDC semantics (and Cosmos DB exposes its own change feed too). For MongoDB drivers, change streams work against accounts configured with a Mongo API version that supports them (Mongo 3.6+). No separate feature flag is normally required for standard accounts, but confirm the account's Mongo version/settings; for the native Cosmos change feed you may need to use the change feed API/SDK.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server profile described in the run environment — it is the MCP server that contains tooling for this DocumentDB/Mongo API endpoint. The general Azure MCP server can manage Azure resources, but the specialized 'documentdb' MCP server is the one with data-plane inspection tools for collections, indexes and query plans for this service.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: 'DocumentDB' was the original name of Microsoft’s managed JSON database offering; it was later rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB. The older "DocumentDB" name refers historically to that service; Azure Cosmos DB is the present, broader multi-model service. The open-source "DocumentDB" project (if referenced) is not the same as the Azure service — the Azure service is a proprietary managed engine exposing multiple APIs (including a MongoDB-compatible API).

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Under the MongoDB API you are typically talking to a Cosmos DB storage engine (a proprietary, globally-distributed engine) with a Mongo wire-protocol compatibility layer. This means standard MongoDB drivers mostly work, but there are behavioral and feature differences (consistency models, certain commands/aggregation stages, transactions across partitions, performance characteristics), so test features you rely on and avoid server-specific features that may be missing.

answers.question: What TTL index definition will this sample use to auto-expire trial entitlement documents?
answers.answer: Create a TTL index on the trial expiration field. Example command I would run: db.trials.createIndex({ trialExpiresAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 0, name: 'ttl_trialExpiresAt' }). This will expire documents once trialExpiresAt <= current time.

answers.question: What constraint must be respected to use multi-document transactions in this cluster?
answers.answer: Transactions require all documents to be in the same logical partition (same shard/partition key) — multi-document ACID transactions across different partition keys are not supported or are severely limited. Implementation: ensure charge events and subscription records share the same partition key value (for example customerId) before using session.startTransaction().

answers.question: How will the sample enforce idempotency to prevent double-billing?
answers.answer: Create a unique index on the idempotency key field and attempt an insert; on duplicate-key error treat the charge as already processed. Example index: db.charges.createIndex({ idempotencyKey: 1 }, { unique: true, partialFilterExpression: { idempotencyKey: { $exists: true } }, name: 'uq_idempotencyKey' }).

answers.question: Exactly how will the sample read the connection string at runtime and what driver options should be set?
answers.answer: Read the URI from environment: const uri = process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI; connect with mongoose/mongodb using TLS and conservative driver options, for example mongoose.connect(uri, { tls: true, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates: false, retryWrites: false, serverSelectionTimeoutMS: 5000 }). Do not log the env var or write it to disk.

answers.question: What command will I try first to create a vector index on the embeddings field in the sample collections?
answers.answer: I will try a Mongo-style createIndex with a 'vector' index spec (as the cluster advertises vector support): db.plans.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_vector_idx', vector: { algorithm: 'HNSW', dims: 1536, metric: 'cosine' } }); If that exact option names fail I'll inspect server error and adjust to the server’s required keys (e.g. 'indexType':'hnsw', 'dimension':1536).
